analysis.one_liner: Lets corporations deduct dividends they pay, ending the double tax on distributed profits.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee and expired with zero cosponsors when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: Corporations currently pay tax on their profits, and shareholders pay tax again on dividends those profits fund. This bill would let corporations deduct every dividend they pay out of their taxable income, so profits distributed to shareholders would be taxed once, at the shareholder level, instead of twice. It offsets some of that loss by raising the withholding tax on dividends paid to foreign investors and by barring funds, real estate trusts, and other pass-through businesses from the deduction.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders of corporations, and the corporations themselves. A deduction equal to dividends paid would sharply cut the corporate tax owed on distributed profits, and the largest shareholders are disproportionately the wealthiest households and institutions.

how_it_helps.text: The bill allows corporations a deduction equal to the dividends they pay during the year, so profits distributed to shareholders would no longer be taxed at the corporate level on top of the shareholder level.
The deduction is limited by a 'qualified dividend account' built up from the corporation's adjusted taxable income, so a corporation can deduct dividends up to roughly what it actually earned.

To recapture part of the cost, the bill raises the withholding tax on dividends paid to nonresident aliens and foreign corporations to 30.4 percent, with exceptions for countries whose treaties provide comparable relief.

Mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, S corporations, cooperatives, and foreign sales corporations are barred from the deduction, since their income already passes to owners without entity-level tax.
When one corporation buys another's assets, the acquiring corporation inherits the target's qualified dividend account, preserving the deduction through mergers.

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers generally. Every dollar of distributed corporate profit would escape corporate tax, reducing federal revenue, while the offsetting withholding increase applies mainly to foreign holders and treaty-country residents.

drawbacks.text: The deduction applies to all dividends paid by corporations, so the tax savings flow to whoever holds the stock — and stock ownership is concentrated among the wealthiest households — while the lost revenue would have to be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing.

The bill adds a new layer of bookkeeping: every corporation must maintain a qualified dividend account with detailed annual adjustments for credits, minimum tax, and reorganizations, which the bill leaves largely to Treasury regulations.

Raising the withholding rate on dividends to foreign holders to 30.4 percent could discourage foreign investment in U.S. stock, which is why the bill carves out treaty countries that offer equivalent relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ending double taxation of dividends is a real policy idea that some economists favor, but this version directs the entire benefit to shareholders of corporations — a group skewed heavily toward the wealthy — while the cost lands on the general Treasury. The revenue offsets cover only dividends paid to foreigners. The bill also carried substantial compliance complexity, and it attracted no cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Shelby introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; it expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Shelby introduced the bill on June 13, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no vote — through the end of the Congress on January 3, 1991.
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill would have cut taxes mainly for corporate shareholders and cost the Treasury revenue, its death left ordinary taxpayers in the same position as before; no concentrated interest gained from the outcome, and the status quo held.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; the tax status quo held

for.role: U.S. Senator from Alabama, bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered no follow-up recorded in the action history.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to and never reported from
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors, so no partisan pattern exists in the record.

industries.note: A deduction equal to dividends paid would remove the corporate-level tax on distributed profits, and stock ownership is concentrated among the wealthiest households. The cost would be lower federal revenue made up by other taxpayers.
Corporations could distribute earnings to owners without paying corporate tax on those amounts, reducing their overall tax burden. Shareholder wealth, not worker wages, is the direct beneficiary.

industries.industry: Mutual funds, REITs, S corporations, and cooperatives
industries.note: The bill bars these pass-through vehicles from the new deduction, but they already escape entity-level tax, so their practical position is largely unchanged while corporate competitors get a new break.
Withholding on dividends to nonresident aliens and foreign corporations would rise to 30.4 percent to recapture the deduction's cost, unless their country's treaty provides equivalent relief.
